q: A label reading Blanc de Blancs tells a guest what about the contents?
opts: It was made entirely from black grapes
It was made only from white grapes
It was bottled with no dosage at all
It spent no time ageing on its lees
exp: White from whites. Chardonnay dominates the category so completely that the terms are used interchangeably, although the rare white varieties are also permitted.

q: Only Pinot Noir and Meunier went into a particular cuvee. Which term belongs on the label?
exp: A white wine pressed from black grapes. Whole-bunch pressing keeps the juice pale, and the results are usually broader and more overtly fruity than a Blanc de Blancs.

q: Late budding offers a measure of insurance against spring frost on low-lying sites. Which of the three main varieties provides it?
exp: Meunier buds later and ripens earlier than Pinot Noir, so it both dodges the frost and finishes ahead of the autumn rain. It gives a blend forward fruit and early drinkability.

q: Beyond the famous three, several near-extinct varieties remain legal in the appellation. Which is one of them?
exp: Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris survive in tiny plantings. A handful of growers now bottle them, often as a single cuvee drawing on all seven permitted varieties.

q: Rose here may legally be produced by a route forbidden in most French appellations. What is it?
opts: Adding red grape skins to the dosage
Fermenting the wine on oak chips
exp: Rose d'assemblage is the common method: the still red goes into the white base before the second fermentation, which gives precise control of colour from year to year. The alternative, rose de saignee, takes its colour from a short maceration on skins instead.

q: Harvesting is done by hand across the whole appellation. Which requirement of the pressing stage explains the rule?
opts: Whole, unbroken bunches must reach the press
The fruit must be crushed in the vineyard
Sorting is forbidden in the cellar
exp: A machine breaks the berries, and broken black grapes bleed colour into the juice. Whole bunches also form their own filter bed, so the press runs gently and the juice comes off clean.

q: From a marc of 4,000 kilograms of grapes, what is the greatest volume of juice that may be taken?
exp: The ceiling works out at about 102 litres per 160 kilograms and is deliberately low. Pressing harder extracts phenolics and colour that a delicate base wine cannot carry.

q: The first 2,050 litres to run from that press carry which name?
exp: The cuvee fraction is the cleanest and most acidic juice and goes into the best wines. The 500 litres of taille that follow are richer, coarser and quicker to age.

q: Some producers block malolactic conversion in their base wines. What are they preserving?
opts: Sharp malic acidity in the base wine
Colour extracted from the black skins
Carbon dioxide from the first fermentation
exp: Malolactic softens malic acid into lactic and adds a creamy note. Blocking it keeps the wine taut, leaner and longer-lived, at the cost of needing more time or a touch more dosage to come into balance.

q: Blending takes place long before the wine ever sparkles. What does assemblage draw together?
opts: Already finished sparkling wines taken after disgorgement
Wines bought in from other French sparkling regions
Wines from a single vineyard in one village only
Different villages, varieties and often several vintages
exp: A large house may taste through hundreds of separate lots in the new year. The blend rather than the vineyard is the traditional unit of quality here, which inverts the Burgundian model.

q: Bottling for the second fermentation includes an addition of sugar and yeast. What is that mixture called?
exp: Still wine, cane sugar and a yeast culture, plus a clarifying agent to help the deposit slide later. The bottle is then sealed under a crown cap and laid down.

q: Trapped carbon dioxide from the second fermentation builds to roughly what pressure?
exp: Five to six bar, comparable to a lorry tyre. Roughly four grams of sugar per litre yields one further atmosphere, and the same fermentation adds a little over one percent alcohol.

q: Brioche, toast and biscuit notes develop while the wine rests on its spent yeast. Which process produces them?
exp: The dead yeast cells break down and release amino acids, mannoproteins and other compounds into the wine. The longer the contact, the deeper the register and the finer the bead.

q: Bottles are turned and progressively tilted over a period of weeks. What does remuage accomplish?
opts: It raises the pressure in the bottle
It works the sediment down into the neck
It dissolves the sediment back into the wine
exp: Hand riddling on a pupitre takes a skilled worker several weeks; a gyropalette handles around five hundred bottles at once in a few days. The bottle ends up inverted, sur pointe.

q: Necks are dipped into a freezing bath before the crown cap comes off. What does that achieve?
opts: It freezes the sediment into a plug
It drives the carbon dioxide out
exp: The pressure in the bottle expels the frozen plug the moment the cap comes off. Degorgement a la glace loses only a mouthful of wine and can be done at speed on a line. The older method a la volee, disgorging unfrozen, is now the minority but stays in real use for magnums and larger formats and among some growers.

q: After disgorgement the bottle is topped up with wine and usually a little sugar. What is that addition called?
exp: Dosage sets the final sweetness and fills the space the ice plug left behind. It is measured in grams of sugar per litre, and the legal categories follow directly from it.
